Question:
Each square in a \(3 \times 3\) grid is randomly filled with one of the \(4\) shaded-and-unshaded tiles shown below on the right.

[Figure 1](figures/2023_AMC_8_Q23_question_fig1.svg)

What is the probability that the tiling will contain a large shaded diamond in one of the smaller \(2 \times 2\) grids? Below is an example of such a tiling.

[Figure 2](figures/2023_AMC_8_Q23_question_fig2.svg)
Solution:
Every smaller \(2\times2\) grid includes the center square of the \(3\times3\) grid. This shared square lets us identify the only possible location of a shaded diamond before counting probabilities.

Each tile has one corner where both meeting sides are shaded. In a large shaded diamond, the four tiles must point those shaded corners toward the same grid vertex, the center of the diamond. Once the center square's tile is chosen, its shaded corner determines which one of the four \(2\times2\) grids could contain the diamond. No other location can work with that center tile.

For this candidate to become a diamond, each of the other three squares around that vertex must have one particular tile orientation. Each has probability \(\frac14\) of matching, independently of the others. The five squares outside the candidate can be filled in any way. Therefore the probability is

\[
\left(\frac14\right)^3=\boxed{\frac1{64}},
\]

choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).

The center tile is already fixed when we test the three matches. There is no additional factor of \(\frac14\) for it, because every orientation of that tile supplies one candidate location.
